title: Module 6: Failure modes, buckling, restraint and stability
shortTitle: Failure modes, buckling, restraint and stability
whyItMatters: Most real structural collapses, especially during construction and temporary works stages, are stability or buckling failures (Euler column buckling, LTB, missing bracing, overturning) rather than simple material overstress.
introduction: Contrasts material-related failure modes (yielding, rupture, crushing, shear, bearing, fatigue, brittle fracture) against stability-related failure modes (local buckling, flexural/torsional buckling, Lateral Torsional Buckling, global sway, overturning, sliding). Covers Euler critical load P_cr = π²EI/L_cr², effective lengths, compression-flange restraint against LTB, building stability systems, and why intermediate construction stages are often more vulnerable than the completed structure.
objectives: Distinguish material strength failures from geometric stability/buckling failures across beams, columns, frames, connections, walls, and foundations.
Calculate Euler buckling loads and explain how end restraints and intermediate bracing change effective length L_cr and critical load P_cr (Example 6.1).
Explain the physical mechanism of Lateral Torsional Buckling (LTB) and what constitutes effective compression-flange or torsional restraint (Example 6.2).
Trace lateral stability systems (braced frames, moment frames, shear walls, diaphragms) and identify construction-stage stability risks (Examples 6.3 and 6.4).
learningGate: List credible failure modes for a beam, column, frame, connection, wall, and foundation.,Distinguish strength failure from stability failure clearly.,Explain Lateral Torsional Buckling (LTB) in your own words without relying on code jargon.,Identify effective length and restraint assumptions and what makes them valid in reality.,Identify a complete lateral load path from wind/notional load to the foundations.

topics.title: Material Failure vs Stability Failure & Euler Column Buckling (Example 6.1)
topics.summary: Contrasts material failures (yielding, crushing, rupture, shear, bearing) with stability failures, derives/applies Euler critical load P_cr = π²EI/L_cr² (Example 6.1), and explains effective length L_cr, slenderness λ = L_cr/i, and why increasing area A alone may not efficiently solve a buckling problem.
subtopics: Material failure modes: yielding, tensile rupture, compression crushing, shear, bearing, fatigue, brittle fracture
Stability failure modes: local plate buckling, flexural column buckling, torsional/flexural-torsional buckling
Euler critical buckling load: P_cr = π² E I / L_cr² (governed by minor-axis I_min unless restrained)
Effective length factors (L_cr / L): pinned-pinned (1.0), fixed-fixed non-sway (0.5), fixed-pinned (0.7), fixed-free cantilever column (2.0)
Syllabus Example 6.1: comparing pinned-pinned vs fixed-fixed columns of equal section and length
Imperfection sensitivity and why real columns buckle below the ideal Euler curve
learningObjectives: Compare Euler buckling loads for different end restraints (Example 6.1) and identify which axis governs.
Explain why increasing second moment of area I (or reducing L_cr) is far more efficient than adding solid area A for slender struts.

questions.learningObjective: Compare Euler buckling load of fixed-fixed vs pinned-pinned column (Example 6.1)
questions.prompt: Compare two ideal elastic columns of identical cross-section (flexural rigidity EI) and physical length L. Column 1 is pinned at both ends (effective length L_cr = 1.0 L) and Column 2 is fully fixed against rotation and sway at both ends (theoretical L_cr = 0.5 L). What is the ratio of their Euler critical buckling loads (P_cr,fixed / P_cr,pinned)?
questions.assumptions: Note: in practical steel design (EN 1993-1-1 / BS 5975), a conservative effective length factor of 0.7L is often used instead of the theoretical 0.5L because real connections are never infinitely rigid.
questions.explanation: Since P_cr = π²EI / L_cr², halving the effective length from 1.0 L to 0.5 L multiplies P_cr by 1 / (0.5)² = 4.0. Step-by-step verification for "Compare Euler buckling load of fixed-fixed vs pinned-pinned column (Example 6.1)": confirm that all input quantities are converted into consistent SI metric units before substitution, evaluate the governing equilibrium or constitutive equation to obtain 4 ratio, and cross-check the magnitude and sign against StructTutor Syllabus Mod 6 (Compression Buckling, LTB & Overall Frame Stability).
questions.citation: Euler Elastic Buckling Theory, Ayrton-Perry Formulation & BS EN 1993-1-1 Cl. 6.3
hints: Identify the governing equilibrium or mechanics equation for "Compare Euler buckling load of fixed-fixed vs pinned-pinned column (Example 6.1)" and convert all given dimensions and loads into consistent SI units (N, mm, or kN, m) before calculating.
Calculation setup: Since P_cr = π²EI / L_cr², halving the effective length from 1.0 L to 0.5 L multiplies P_cr by 1 / (0.5)² = ?. Express your final numeric answer in ratio.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate Euler critical load P_cr of a pinned-pinned strut
questions.prompt: A 3,000 mm long pin-ended steel strut has E = 210,000 N/mm² and minor-axis second moment of area I_z = 4.5 × 10⁶ mm⁴ (with major-axis I_y = 18.0 × 10⁶ mm⁴ and no intermediate restraints). Calculate its Euler critical buckling load P_cr = π² E I_min / L_cr² in kN (to 1 decimal place).
questions.assumptions: Always use the minimum I_z (or largest slenderness L_cr / i) when effective lengths about both axes are equal.
questions.explanation: An unrestrained pin-ended strut buckles about its weakest axis (I_z = 4.5 × 10⁶ mm⁴). P_cr = (π² × 210,000 × 4.5 × 10⁶) / 3,000² = (9.8696 × 9.45 × 10¹¹) / (9.0 × 10⁶) = 1,036,308 N ≈ 1,036.3 kN.
questions.citation: Euler Elastic Buckling Theory, Ayrton-Perry Formulation & BS EN 1993-1-1 Cl. 6.3
hints: Identify the governing equilibrium or mechanics equation for "Calculate Euler critical load P_cr of a pinned-pinned strut" and convert all given dimensions and loads into consistent SI units (N, mm, or kN, m) before calculating.
Calculation setup: An unrestrained pin-ended strut buckles about its weakest axis (I_z = 4.5 × 10⁶ mm⁴). Express your final numeric answer in kN.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate Euler buckling load of a freestanding flagpole/cantilever column
questions.prompt: A 3,000 mm long steel strut (E = 210,000 N/mm², governing minor-axis I_z = 4.5 × 10⁶ mm⁴, giving P_cr = 1,036.3 kN when pin-ended with L_cr = L) is instead fixed at its base and completely free to translate and rotate at its top (cantilever column with L_cr = 2.0 L = 6,000 mm). Calculate its Euler critical buckling load P_cr in kN (to 1 decimal place).
questions.assumptions: Shows why unbraced freestanding cantilever columns have 4 times lower elastic buckling capacity than braced pin-ended columns.
questions.explanation: Doubling L_cr from 1.0 L to 2.0 L divides P_cr by 2² = 4: 1,036.3 / 4 = 259.08 kN ≈ 259.1 kN. questions.learningObjective: Explain why increasing area A alone may not efficiently solve a buckling problem
questions.prompt: A slender solid circular steel rod is failing by elastic Euler buckling under axial compression. Why is switching to a hollow circular tube of larger outer diameter (with an equal cross-sectional area A) much more effective at increasing buckling resistance than using a slightly thicker solid bar?
questions.assumptions: Explicit syllabus Learn point under Buckling fundamentals.
options: Because hollow tubes have a higher Young’s modulus E than solid rods, assuming that because the maximum principal tensile stress under pure shear equals the uniaxial yield strength according to the Rankine maximum normal stress hypothesis, which governs brittle fracture in unreinforced cast iron and uncracked plain concrete elements rather than ductile structural steel

Because elastic buckling is governed by second moment of area I (and radius of gyration i = √(I/A)), not area A alone; moving the steel outward into a hollow tube dramatically increases I and i without adding weight
Because Euler’s formula P_cr = π²EI/L_cr² does not depend on I

Because Eurocode partial safety factors for resistance incorporate a statistical log-normal coefficient of variation for hot-rolled plate thickness tolerances, mill rolling residual stresses, and out-of-straightness bow imperfections across the member length
questions.explanation: In Euler buckling, yield strength fy does not appear and area A only helps to the extent that it increases I = A·i². Spreading material away from the centroid maximises i.
questions.citation: Euler Elastic Buckling Theory, Ayrton-Perry Formulation & BS EN 1993-1-1 Cl. 6.3
hints: Consider the physical load path, equilibrium boundary conditions, and deformation compatibility for "Explain why increasing area A alone may not efficiently solve a buckling problem". Distinguish carefully between ULS strength/stability checks and SLS deflection/cracking behaviour.
Engineering principle check: eliminate options that violate static equilibrium, ignore construction-stage instability, or confuse elastic stiffness (E·I) with material yield strength (f_y).

questions.learningObjective: Explain why real columns fail below the ideal Euler buckling load
questions.prompt: Why does a real structural steel column of intermediate slenderness buckle at an axial load significantly lower than both the squash load (A·f_y) and the theoretical Euler load (π²EI/L_cr²)?
options: Because gravity acts horizontally on intermediate columns, assuming that it redistributes the peak hogging bending moment into the adjacent midspan zone through rigid-plastic hinge rotation without requiring supplementary lateral-torsional restraint, web stiffeners, or ductile rotation capacity at the support interface

It increases the elastic Euler critical buckling load by halving the effective buckling length between inflection points, provided that the connection detail transfers full axial thrust without slip or local web crippling

Because real columns contain initial geometric out-of-straightness (bow imperfections), residual stresses locked in from hot-rolling/welding, and minor load eccentricities that induce bending and early yielding on the concave side before P_cr is reached

It eliminates vertical shear deformation across the web depth by forcing the neutral axis to remain coincident with the geometric centroid of the uncracked transformed section throughout both construction and permanent service stages
questions.explanation: Initial bow e₀ creates a second-order bending moment P·(e₀ + δ) that causes the concave compression flange to yield and lose tangent stiffness E_t before reaching the elastic bifurcation load P_cr.

topics.title: Lateral Torsional Buckling (LTB) & Effective Restraint (Example 6.2)
topics.summary: Covers the physical mechanism of Lateral Torsional Buckling (compression flange buckling sideways accompanied by twisting of the cross-section), effective restraint points, torsional restraint at supports, and destabilising top-flange loads (Example 6.2).
subtopics: Physical mechanism of LTB: the compression flange behaves like a strut, buckles laterally between restraints, and twists the beam cross-section
Syllabus Example 6.2: sketching tension flange, compression flange, lateral displacement, twisting, and restraint points
What constitutes true lateral restraint: must restrain the COMPRESSION flange (or prevent twist) back to a braced node
Why bottom-flange restraint alone does not prevent top-flange LTB in a sagging beam (unless combined with stiff web/torsional restraint)
Destabilising loads applied to the top compression flange without lateral restraint
learningObjectives: Explain LTB in plain physical terms and identify which flange requires restraint in sagging vs hogging regions (Example 6.2).
Recognise when a floor/purlin detail does or does not provide effective LTB restraint.

questions.learningObjective: Explain Lateral Torsional Buckling (LTB) physically (Example 6.2 & Module 6 Gate)
questions.prompt: When a long, deep steel I-beam is bent about its strong (major) axis under downward gravity load without intermediate lateral bracing, what happens physically during Lateral Torsional Buckling (LTB)?
questions.assumptions: Core Module 6 Gate requirement and Example 6.2.
options: The bottom tension flange buckles sideways while the top flange stretches, assuming that the member is verified solely for Ultimate Limit State cross-sectional yield resistance at midspan while relying on friction alone at the bearings to resist horizontal thermal expansion, wind drag, and notional lateral equivalent forces
The beam shears cleanly in half vertically at the support without any sideways movement

The design substitutes the characteristic 95th-percentile material strength in place of the 5th-percentile characteristic strength and omits the combination factor ψ_0 when superimpose-combining independent variable wind and imposed floor actions

The top flange is in axial compression and behaves like a slender column; it buckles sideways (laterally) about its weak minor axis while the tension bottom flange stays straighter, forcing the whole cross-section to twist torsionally and lose bending capacity before reaching full yield
questions.explanation: LTB is a coupled lateral-buckling and twisting instability of a beam bent about its major axis when its compression flange is not adequately restrained laterally.
questions.citation: Euler Elastic Buckling Theory, Ayrton-Perry Formulation & BS EN 1993-1-1 Cl. 6.3

questions.learningObjective: Identify what is required for a restraint to effectively prevent LTB
questions.prompt: A simply supported steel beam is in sagging bending under gravity load. An engineer claims the beam is "fully laterally restrained" because timber joists rest loose on top of the top flange with no fixings and no bracing bay at the ends of the building. Why is this assumption unsafe?
questions.assumptions: Directly links Module 6 LTB to Module 8 and Module 17 detailing.
options: Effective LTB restraint requires both positive connection to the compression flange (or torsional restraint) AND a stiff lateral load path (diaphragm or plan bracing) that transfers the restraint force (e.g. 2.5% of flange force) back to a braced line; unfixed loose members can simply slide or move sideways with the buckling flange

By applying the unfactored characteristic Serviceability Limit State action combination directly to the gross cross-sectional area without accounting for partial material safety factors, second-order geometric imperfections, or local buckling slenderness reductions at the critical section when evaluated under unfactored.
Sagging beams only require restraint to the bottom tension flange

By taking the mean 50th-percentile material stiffness modulus together with a fully fixed rotational boundary condition at both ends, thereby ignoring connection flexibility, long-term creep deformation, and differential support settlement under sustained gravity loading
questions.explanation: A restraint is only as good as its connection to the compression flange and the stiffness of the bracing system it ties back to. Engineering synthesis for "Identify what is required for a restraint to effectively prevent LTB": always trace the complete load path from point of application to the foundations, ensure compatibility between analysis boundary assumptions and physical site detailing, and verify against StructTutor Syllabus Mod 6 (Compression Buckling, LTB & Overall Frame Stability).

questions.learningObjective: Identify which flange is the compression flange in a cantilever or hogging region
questions.prompt: In a cantilever steel beam under downward gravity load (or over the internal support of a continuous beam), which flange is in compression and therefore vulnerable to Lateral Torsional Buckling?
options: Because the maximum principal tensile stress under pure shear equals the uniaxial yield strength according to the Rankine maximum normal stress hypothesis, which governs brittle fracture in unreinforced cast iron and uncracked plain concrete elements rather than ductile structural steel
The bottom flange (so a roof deck fixed only to the top tension flange does NOT automatically restrain the bottom compression flange against LTB unless torsional fly-bracing is provided)

Because the elastic shear modulus G is related to Young’s modulus E by G = E / [2(1 + ν)], which introduces a Poisson’s ratio reduction factor across the web depth whenever transverse direct stresses are neglected in simple beam theory

Because Eurocode partial safety factors for resistance incorporate a statistical log-normal coefficient of variation for hot-rolled plate thickness tolerances, mill rolling residual stresses, and out-of-straightness bow imperfections across the member length
questions.explanation: In hogging (-M), the bottom flange is in compression and the top flange is in tension. Assuming top-flange roof decking restrains the bottom flange in a hogging portal haunch or cantilever without fly-stays is a classic design error!

questions.learningObjective: Understand destabilising load-height effect on an unrestrained top flange
questions.prompt: Why is a downward gravity point load applied to the top flange of a laterally unrestrained steel I-beam (destabilising load application) more severe for Lateral Torsional Buckling than an identical gravity load suspended from the bottom tension flange?
questions.assumptions: Crucial concept in temporary works runway beams and unrestrained lintels.
options: It redistributes the peak hogging bending moment into the adjacent midspan zone through rigid-plastic hinge rotation without requiring supplementary lateral-torsional restraint, web stiffeners, or ductile rotation capacity at the support interface when evaluated under unfactored serviceability actions across the gross cross-section without partial safety factors or second-order geometric slenderness reductions
Because loads on the top flange double the vertical support reactions

When the beam begins to twist during LTB, a vertical load sitting on the top flange moves sideways outside the shear centre and creates an additional twisting torque that amplifies the rotation (destabilising load), whereas a load hanging from the bottom flange pulls it back toward vertical
Because bottom-flange loads eliminate vertical shear force

questions.learningObjective: Compare sway resistance in unbraced, diagonally braced, and moment frames (Example 6.3)
questions.prompt: A horizontal wind load H acts at roof eaves level on three single-storey frames with pinned column bases: Frame 1 has pinned beam-to-column joints and no bracing; Frame 2 has pinned joints with a diagonal tension brace; Frame 3 has rigid moment-resisting beam-to-column joints. How does each frame resist lateral sway?
options: All three frames resist H purely by axial compression in the beam, assuming that the member is verified solely for Ultimate Limit State cross-sectional yield resistance at midspan while relying on friction alone at the bearings to resist horizontal thermal expansion, wind drag, and notional lateral equivalent forces
Frame 1 is the stiffest because it has no diagonal brace

The design substitutes the characteristic 95th-percentile material strength in place of the 5th-percentile characteristic strength and omits the combination factor ψ_0 when superimpose-combining independent variable wind and imposed floor actions

Frame 1 collapses sideways as a four-hinge sway mechanism; Frame 2 resists H efficiently via axial tension in the diagonal brace and axial forces in the columns/rafter (truss action); Frame 3 resists H by developing bending moments and shear in the columns and beam via the rigid knee joints
questions.explanation: Braced frames resist sway by axial triangulation (stiff and efficient), while moment frames resist sway by flexural bending of columns and beams (requiring stiff moment connections and deeper columns/beams).

questions.learningObjective: Calculate tension in a diagonal brace of a single-storey braced bay
questions.prompt: A single-storey braced bay of width B = 4.0 m and height H = 3.0 m (diagonal length D = 5.0 m) resists a horizontal wind load of F_w = 24 kN at eaves level via a single tension diagonal running from the bottom-left pin to the top-right eaves node. Calculate the axial tension force T in the diagonal brace in kN.
questions.assumptions: The vertical component T × sin(θ) = 30 × (3/5) = 18 kN induces uplift at the windward column base and compression in the leeward column.
questions.explanation: Horizontal equilibrium at the top node: T × cos(θ) = F_w, where cos(θ) = B / D = 4.0 / 5.0 = 0.80. Thus T = 24 / 0.80 = 30.0 kN. moduleAssessmentQuestions.learningObjective: Explain why falsework towers require plan bracing and diagonal lacing in TWO orthogonal directions
moduleAssessmentQuestions.prompt: A temporary works engineer designs a row of heavily loaded falsework props laced together with diagonal bracing in the North–South plane, but omits bracing in the East–West plane. What will happen under vertical concrete load?
moduleAssessmentQuestions.assumptions: Essential 3D stability principle.
options: Bracing in one plane automatically restrains buckling in the perpendicular plane, assuming that it redistributes the peak hogging bending moment into the adjacent midspan zone through rigid-plastic hinge rotation without requiring supplementary lateral-torsional restraint, web stiffeners, or ductile rotation capacity at the support interface

It increases the elastic Euler critical buckling load by halving the effective buckling length between inflection points, provided that the connection detail transfers full axial thrust without slip or local web crippling
The props will buckle effortlessly out-of-plane in the unbraced East–West direction at their full unbraced height
Nothing; compression struts only buckle in one direction
moduleAssessmentQuestions.explanation: A 3D column or prop will always seek the path of least resistance (largest L_cr / i); bracing in one plane leaves the perpendicular plane completely unrestrained unless braced in both x and y planes.

moduleAssessmentQuestions.learningObjective: Recognise brittle fracture risk in thick welded steelwork at low temperature

options: Because cold temperatures reduce Young’s modulus E to zero, assuming that the member is verified solely for Ultimate Limit State cross-sectional yield resistance at midspan while relying on friction alone at the bearings to resist horizontal thermal expansion, wind drag, and notional lateral equivalent forces

Because brittle fracture only happens at temperatures above 500°C
